VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic

We can compare this with the thirty birds (sî-morgh) standing before the eternal Simurgh. Here the eternal Simurgh is the Dator formarum. What we have is neither the confusion of all things into an undifferentiated whole nor an opposition or confrontation between one being and another, but 1 × 1. This symbol is the supreme formula of dualitude: it preserves unity of essence without confusion of persons—or, in this case, without confusion of “images.” These are not two separate ones added together (1 + 1) to make two. They are two ones that, precisely by multiplying one another (1 × 1), make only one One. This is the symbolic number, the “cipher,” of esoteric tawhîd that we shall encounter again in Ruzbihan of Shiraz (see below, Book III). If this is the secret of the Dator formarum rediscovered at the heart of the “Personal City,” it is also the secret of forms and their transformations that the mystical pilgrim has thereby won.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic

And perhaps it is only after reaching this level of spiritual awareness that the pilgrim can understand the true daring of transformation: a daring that saves him from the catastrophe and disintegration of Forms, from the sterile turmoil of formlessness that we ourselves witness in every sphere today. For such daring unfolds only in souls that Sufism, under various names, calls souls of desire. The story of a soul of desire, as our little Indo-Iranian romance has suggested alongside many others, begins long before the soul enters this world. In that origin lies the inner law belonging to that soul alone, together with its foreknowledge of the new form that has always been its own and no one else’s.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic

But to what extent can our world, having broken with faith and hope, still understand—how can we avoid asking?—that for each of us, each unique being, the only truly new being is the one who guides us, and that this being can guide us only because it existed before us? And that this being, new and yet pre-eternal, is the only one who, “if we entrust it with our thought, will at last bring to fulfillment our most secret thought—the one that no one before us ever expressed, and that we ourselves did not so much think as feel, so completely did it live within us as one with love” .
1. The Spiritual Legacy of the “Royal Road”

The preceding chapters have shown how the Shaykh al-Ishrâq put his “great idea” into practice: the creation of a complete spiritual culture, one that embraces the whole of philosophical knowledge while directing it toward the full spiritual realization of the human person. The path of Ishrâq—the “Eastern” theosophy revived from ancient Persia—turns neither right nor left.

Whoever sets out upon it is called to be neither a theoretical philosopher who forgets philosophy's true purpose nor a mystical adventurer unaware of the dangers facing anyone whom philosophy has not yet awakened to self-knowledge or protected against illusions of every kind. This is why the path may be called the “royal road” (hê basilikê hodos).

I borrow the expression here from the mystical theosophy of Philo of Alexandria. Although our “Eastern” theosophers did not know his work, it too would invite many comparisons with theirs. Such comparisons would extend those that others have already drawn between Philo's divine “Powers” and the Amahraspands, the Archangels of the Avesta.

The expression royal road comes from the Book of Numbers: “We will follow the royal road, turning neither right nor left, until we have passed through your territory” (20:17 and 21:22). This “royal road” is the path of gnosis, of knowledge attained through direct vision. It is the path of the “race of seers,” and it leads them to the highest degree: the apotheôsis that Sohrawardî calls ta’alloh, becoming godlike. It is the path that brings the “exile” back to the summit of the mystical Sinai, where the entrance to the “eighth clime” opens before him.

The royal road is also what the gnostics of Islam call the “Straight Path” (sîrât mostaqîm). It turns neither right nor left: it is a path along the mountain ridge, where the virtues cultivated on both slopes come together and reach their height. Sohrawardî's great idea left a profound mark on Iran's spiritual culture. There have certainly been theoretical philosophers, and there have been Sufis who disdained philosophy. Neither group, taken alone, embodies that spiritual culture in its fullness.

We have already heard the testimony of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî (see below, Book V, Chapter II): “What is most fitting is for the pilgrim journeying toward God to bring the two methods together. His inner discipline should never be without philosophical meditation; and, conversely, his philosophical meditation should never be without an effort of spiritual purification. Better still, his spiritual method should be a barzakh—an intermediate realm joining the two methods. Such is the path followed by the Hokamâ’ ishrâqîyûn, the ‘Eastern’ theosophers (the ‘Platonists of Persia’).” Thus the spiritual teaching intended by Sohrawardî has continued from century to century.

And the name “royal road” is all the more appropriate because its emblematic hero was Kay Khosraw, the wise and visionary king who, by taking this path, brought Iran's heroic epic to its culmination as a mystical epic. He is its emblematic hero because all the sages of ancient Persia who follow him along this “royal road” are themselves named after him: they are the khosrawânîyûn, a term that, in Sohrawardî's thought, is equivalent to Ishrâqîyûn.

We now know the importance Sohrawardî attached to this name and to the role of Kay Khosraw. The meaning he gives to Kay Khosraw's example and to the designation khosrawânîyûn confirms his most explicit statements about his purpose in reviving the mystical theosophy of the ancient Persian sages. If these sages were “Eastern”—in the sense of Ishrâqîyûn—it was because they were khosrawânîyûn. This is the meaning and significance of what we might call Sohrawardî's Iranism. Its wholly spiritual and “hieratic,” or sacred, character becomes clear.

This is the first time we have used the word Iranism here. It might have found a place in one of the great systems of the “philosophy of history” developed in the West, had Sohrawardî's work been known there. In fact, there is one such system in which Iranism appears, raised almost to the status of a metaphysical principle.

But the philosophical system in question was produced by a school little known in Western Europe except among specialists. I am thinking of the circle known as the “Slavophiles” in Russia during the first half of the nineteenth century. Perhaps it is no geographical accident that this was where the principle of Iranism bore fruit in philosophy. Unfortunately, the Iranian philosophers of the time seem to have had no opportunity to learn about it; nor have subsequent circumstances done much to draw their attention to a school whose Iranism directly concerns them.

Elsewhere we have already had occasion to suggest both the affinities and the contrasts between the Iranism of Alexis Khomiakov and that of Sohrawardî. We know that a whole book would be needed to pursue the comparison: the field remains completely unexplored. Here I wish only to add briefly to the suggestions made earlier.

In the magnificent philosophy of history constructed by Alexis Khomiakov—a philosophy that owes nothing to Hegelian dialectic—two principles, two types of civilization, confront one another from humanity's first steps into history. On one side stands the principle of freedom, expressed in creation; on the other, the principle of necessity, expressed in generation. Khomiakov gives these two principles names that almost personify them. Iranism is the creative spiritual principle, the religion of moral freedom.

Kushism (Kush is the biblical name for Ethiopia) is the religion of physical as well as logical necessity. Kushism knows only the necessary sequence of logical reasoning; in this sense it finds its fullest expression in Hegel's system. Iranism, or Iranian thought, “rests upon tradition and cannot be restored by a purely logical operation, for the idea of creative freedom cannot be enclosed in formulas or deduced from them. It can be discerned only through a higher intuition, beyond the narrow limits of reasoning, or through the labor of centuries that have passed through every stage of negation.”

Might we not say that, in Sohrawardî's thought, Kushism is represented by the philosophy of the Peripatetics—the rule of Logic, the necessity imposed by the laws of rational understanding? What Hegel represented to Khomiakov, Peripatetic philosophy, if not Aristotle himself, represented to Sohrawardî.

And the rule of logical necessity, like that of physical necessity, is broken by the visionary theosophy of Iran's Khosrawânîyûn: by the free ascent of vision, which gives shape to what it sees; by the “higher intuition” that enters spiritual worlds barred to the dialectic of Logic. The affirmation of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world, is thus a paradoxical act. By daring to “step outside” the constraints of empiricism and the supposed certainties of rational Logic, it overcomes the opposition between them.

Khomiakov speaks of having “passed through every stage of negation.” Sohrawardî, for his part, is as opposed to the Peripatetics as anyone could be, yet he requires his disciple first to pass through every stage of Peripatetic philosophy, through the world of Logic. He does this himself throughout the first part of the Book of Eastern Theosophy, although under a Stoic inspiration in which interpretation takes precedence over dialectic.

Logic is thereby simplified and broken open, and the book arrives at a metaphysics of vision. The Kushite principle is not overcome by simply going around it or leaving it untouched. Perhaps Khomiakov's inspired intuition would take an unexpected turn if it were examined more closely alongside the purpose of Sohrawardî, the “resurrector” of ancient Iran's theosophical wisdom.

To be sure, what mattered to Khomiakov was not geographical, historical, or even ethnic fact, but the religious principle—or rather, the struggle between two principles that makes up the drama of humanity's spiritual history.

Nevertheless, his philosophy also seeks to raise to universal significance the type concealed in the very roots of a people's life: in this case, the Russian type. Even though he and the other Slavophiles were concerned above all with the Russian people's vocation as the exemplary people of Orthodoxy, their thought may also contain a latent concern for a worldly ideal, what has been called a deep-seated “populism.”

Nothing could be further from Sohrawardî's Iranism. He has shown us that the Iranian people, simply as a people, did not thereby deserve to be called “Eastern” in his sense of the word. The knowledge of their ancient sages was not “Eastern” merely because they lived in the geographical East. The reverse is true: it was “Eastern” knowledge that made these Iranians the “Easterners” par excellence. The light of this “East” is the Light of Glory (Xvarnah), which may invest a person or withdraw from one.

The “Eastern” ancestry Sohrawardî claims for himself and his followers is not an ethnic lineage but a hieratic, or sacred, lineage—in the Neoplatonic sense of the word. It lies outside the causal relationships between peoples and states. The grounds on which this lineage rests, like those of the line of guardians of the Grail, belong to a history that breaks through what we ordinarily call history.

The comparison should therefore turn to a different figure: Constantin Leontiev, who placed his faith not in Russia or its people but in the sacred and hieratic ideal of the Byzantine world. He had no interest in providing a mystical foundation for a worldly theocratic kingdom. Insofar as sacred Byzantium inherited the legacy of the Neoplatonists whose “hieratic” wisdom we invoked at the beginning of this study, Sohrawardî's purpose lends itself to comparison with Leontiev's wholly spiritual and ascetic purpose.

For neither man is a people, in itself, what matters most; what matters is the sacred idea that inhabits and governs it. What the sacred idea of Byzantium was to Leontiev, the idea of ancient Iran's theosophical wisdom was to Sohrawardî. Here, too, we could see at work the principle of freedom embodied by Iranism in Khomiakov's drama of the philosophy of history.

No one was more revolutionary and more traditionalist at once than Sohrawardî. He declared that he had no predecessor; yet it was through him, and beginning with him, that the “Eastern” tradition, the ishrâqî tradition, came into existence as a link between the spirituality of ancient Iran and that of Islamic Iran.

It was therefore not without irony that I recently read a criticism directed at a fellow scholar for classifying Sohrawardî among the Sufis. The objection was that Sohrawardî was a Hellenizing philosopher with no connection to any “regularly constituted” Sufi tarîqat, or spiritual order.

Yet the name “Hellenizing philosophers” is generally given to precisely those whom Sohrawardî excludes from the “royal road,” because they were philosophers and nothing more. He himself, then, cannot be one of these “Hellenizing philosophers.” As for making membership in Sufism depend on some unspecified certificate, document, or formal initiation, such a canonical and bureaucratic view is a Western obsession, alien to Sohrawardî's “Easterners.” Sohrawardî did not merely point to the “regular” tradition with which he was connected: he brought it to life.

Spiritual lineage is something witnessed in a person's life. It cannot be proven by archival documents, but by the way of being, living, and thinking that a person takes as a model. There has been, and still is, in Iran an entire Sufism outside Sufism: a spiritual tradition that does not bear the name, sometimes refuses it, and prefers the words ’irfân and ’orafâ’, referring to mystical knowledge and those who possess it. There are “regularly constituted” Shiite Sufi orders.

But there are also others that have never left, and never will leave, traces in any historical archive. That does not in the least prevent their “members” from being Sufis in the true sense of the word. Sohrawardî received the spiritual legacy he left to his followers from an authority infinitely higher than any “regularly constituted” order. The tarîqat of the Ishrâqîyûn, in turn, has no archives.

Sohrawardî left it to his followers to discover his spiritual legacy on the “royal road,” on one condition alone: that they set out upon it. Their commitment depends not on external formalities but on an inward calling. He expressly recalls this calling as he concludes the Book of Eastern Theosophy, in the “testament” addressed to those who will carry on his work.

This testament is prepared for by the closing pages of the book, which I shall now briefly describe. They confirm that the Book of Eastern Theosophy was not intended as a theoretical treatise, not even a treatise on angels. Its purpose is practical: it must be used as an instrument of meditation and spiritual realization. Theological and theosophical “theorems” correspond to psycho-spiritual energies capable of sustaining that realization and receiving it as a gift.

There is a relationship between the appearances of angels and the intensity of the mystic's spiritual life, a relationship that makes each person's experience uniquely his own. The penultimate chapter of Book V, just before the “Testament,” begins an experiential verification of the books that precede it. It is introduced by two “psalms” whose lyrical inspiration briefly interrupts the course of the final part of the work.

But the author warns us that anyone wishing to know the hidden meaning of these psalms must learn it from the person he calls the “Upholder of the Book” —a figure who will be mentioned again in the Testament's final lines. We hesitate, therefore, to press the matter further.

Yet their secret must be very close to that of the Book of Hours (wâridât wa taqdîsât), two of whose “psalms” we translated and discussed above (Chapter III, section 5). Their otherworldly resonance announces the events of ecstasy, always on the point of occurring. It harmonizes with the Manichaean sound of other psalms by Sohrawardî: “Draw the litany of Light upward; deliver the people of Light; lead the Light toward the Light.”

Of the two psalms, or “inspired utterances” (wâridât), that appear at the end of the Book of Eastern Theosophy, I shall quote the opening of the first: “The wanderers who knock at the gateway of the lofty halls of Light, in uprightness and steadfastness of heart, behold, the angels of God come to meet them and draw them toward the Orient of Lights. They greet them with the greetings of the world of the Malakût; they pour over them Water rising from the spring of Beauty, so that they may be made pure.” When this lyrical surge subsides, the exposition resumes with a description of the experiences of those who follow the spiritual path (§ 272).

The commentators, Qotboddîn Shîrâzî and Shahrazôrî, take this opportunity to remind us that the author personally verified not only every theoretical problem discussed in the book but also every genuinely illuminative state he mentions. These states refer to experiences he actually underwent: the fifteen kinds of light and sudden radiance that shake the mystic, from the beginner's stage through the intermediate stage to the first degree of spiritual perfection; the secondary phenomena that accompany them, such as sounds; their seemingly contradictory character, both painful and delightful; the inward vision of one's being brought to white heat; and so on.

All this is described concisely, in a vocabulary of striking precision. Comparison is unavoidable with similar experiences—visions of Lights—described by Najmoddîn Kobrâ (d. 1220), ’Alâoddawleh Semnânî (d. 1336), and Sayyed Mohammad Nûrbakhsh (d. 1464). “When the divine Lights have multiplied upon a human being, they clothe him in the robe of power and majesty, and souls allow themselves to be guided by him” (§ 277). The word Xvarnah does not appear.

But we have already observed, in discussing these lines, that these are the very terms Sohrawardî uses elsewhere to describe the investiture with the royal Xvarnah bestowed upon the life of the mystic: the pilgrim falls beneath the assault of the archangelic Lights—and rises again as a king. This transformation of one's being through the sudden radiance of the Xvarnah, the Light of Glory, corresponds to the Event personally experienced by the mystic in the Malakût, the spiritual kingdom. We have seen how much importance Sohrawardî attaches to the person and ecstasy of Hermes. These lines are like an echo of the Ars Regia, the Royal Art of the Hermetic philosophers.

Finally come the solemn words of the spiritual testament (already discussed above, Chapter I, section 2). Before silence returns, they remind us that this book cannot be studied like any other book. Its aim is not merely to communicate knowledge, but to bring about a real event in the soul—the very event Sohrawardî describes in his initiatory tales: crossing the mountain of Qâf, reaching the mystical Sinai, in short, traveling the “royal road.”

“Brothers, I bequeath to you, as my testament, the observance of God's commands, renunciation of the things He forbids, the complete turning of your being toward God, our Lord, the Light of Lights, abstention from every action and word that is not your concern, and the rejection of every suggestion of the devil. I entrust this Book to your care. Watch over it; protect it from the profane, who are unworthy of it.

“By God, let it take my place—be my ‘caliph’—among you. I finished composing it at the end of the month of Jomâdâ II in the year 582 (16 September 1186), on the day when the seven planets were gathered in the sign of Libra, toward the close of the day. Hand it on only to someone worthy of it, someone who has demonstrated a firm knowledge of Peripatetic philosophy while keeping a heart filled with love for the divine Light.

“Once that condition is fulfilled, before beginning to study the book, the seeker must undertake a forty-day spiritual retreat, abstaining from all meat, eating only the bare minimum, setting aside every concern except meditation upon the Light of God, and following everything prescribed by the Upholder of the Book. When the appointed period before beginning the study of the book has passed, let him then immerse himself in that study” (§§ 278–280).

The Shaykh al-Ishrâq's overriding concern as he completes his book is therefore that it should be placed only in the hands of someone seeking the “royal road”: someone who has passed through the entire course of Peripatetic philosophy, yet whose heart holds a love strong enough to carry him beyond it and free him from the closed circle of theoretical and outwardly apparent certainties.

The commentators say that only those who long to enter the path of direct experience leading to the Orient of Lights may be admitted to the “community of the Book of Eastern Theosophy” (ahl hadhâ'l-kitâb). Those words have a curious affinity with the Quranic expression ahl al-Kitâb, the communities of the Book, as though the Ishrâqîyûn regarded the Book of Eastern Theosophy as itself a book “sent down from heaven.” The “Upholder of the Book” is mentioned again; he will be mentioned once more at the very end.
As for the forty-day retreat prescribed in a few words by the Shaykh as preparation for studying the book, the commentators supply the details.

First, the seeker must attend to the medical care and cleanliness of the body; choose a hermitage sheltered from human noise and concerns, a place of prayer lit only by a subdued light; follow a vegetarian diet; and break the fast only after the evening Prayer, with food that is modest in quantity but delicately prepared—white bread, grains, seasoned greens, almonds, walnuts, and sesame oil. The person on retreat should use carefully chosen perfumes both on the body and in the place of prayer.

Through dhikr, the remembrance of God, whether entirely inward or spoken aloud, the mind should remain occupied day and night with the presence of God, the Angels, and the Archangels of the higher heavenly hierarchies. Elsewhere, in the Creed of the Philosophers, the Shaykh suggests that meditation may be aided by melodies sung softly, the contemplation of suitable images, and so forth. The seeker should spend long periods contemplating the self, “the soul,” as though it had already left behind the dimensions of ordinary time and space and recovered the immaterial nature (tajarrod) of its pure essence.

Sohrawardî himself had many visions of this kind. They led him to defend the power of Imagination as a way of knowing, and the reality of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world: visions of beings from the spiritual world appearing in forms whose beauty surpasses every other beauty.

Qotboddîn Shîrâzî sums the matter up in words identical to Shahrazôrî's: “If the soul perseveres long enough in contemplating itself, behold, a flash of light bursts upon it. This is a light flowing from the archangelic Intelligence upon the soul, an exquisite light that passes like a flash of ecstasy. The Shaykh [Sohrawardî] has described in detail the experience of the different suprasensory lights. Next comes a light that sets the physical organism ablaze [to inward sight]; then a light that wipes away, that abolishes, every awareness in the soul except awareness of its eternal Beloved.

“And this is the ultimate mystical degree.” In another context, this degree appears as the third of the states of mystical consciousness: first, there are you and I; then, I and not you; finally, you and not I. It is toward this ultimate degree that the pilgrim travels along the royal road. That is why Sohrawardî concludes his Creed of the Philosophers with these words: “They have the overflowing portion and the highest rank in this world and the world beyond.

“Blessed is the one who has known himself before dying and has attained for himself in this world a degree that, having made him happy in the abode of passing things, will be his joy in the abode of what endures forever.”

And the testament of the Book of Eastern Theosophy ends with these lines: “Whoever studies this book deeply will recognize that the ancients and the moderns alike have missed something that God has allowed my tongue to express. This book was inspired in my heart all at once by the Holy Spirit, on a wondrous day, although it took me no fewer than several months to write it, because of the difficulties caused by my travels. It deals with a matter of the utmost gravity. If anyone denies that this is so, he will not escape the wrath of God, for God is mighty and has the power to exact retribution (3:3).
“But let no one aspire to know the secrets of this book without turning to the person who is a caliph possessed of the knowledge of the Book (13:43 and 27:40).”

These lines are full of allusions that the commentators help us bring to light. The “something” missed by ancients and moderns alike is the way of the “Eastern” theosophers, the Ishrâqîyûn: the royal road, the middle way that unites and encompasses the philosophers' theoretical and outward knowledge and the inward attainment of spiritual realization. It is something that neither the philosophers of Islam—al-Fârâbî, Avicenna, and others—could reach through philosophy alone, nor the Sufis through spiritual discipline alone.

That is why the book concerns so grave a matter, and why anyone who denies either its gravity or its author's claim exposes himself to divine retribution. This testament is entirely in keeping with the hierarchy of sages established in the book's prologue (above, Chapter II, section 3), with its reference to the unbroken and hidden succession of sages.

At the summit of that hierarchy stands the mysterious figure of the mystical Pole, always present in this world even when entirely unknown to humankind. We had noticed that not a word would need changing for a Shiite reader to recognize here the Twelfth Imam, “invisible to bodily eyes, present in the hearts of his faithful.”
Indeed, the Shaykh al-Ishrâq's testament directs his followers to the mysterious “Upholder of the Book.”

Let us recall again that this is the title above all others that the Imams of Shiism have claimed for themselves. They are the “Upholders of the Book” because they possess both its outward and its inward meaning, the complete art of interpretation that makes the Imam the “speaking Quran.”

This meeting of Shiite and ishrâqî language is not accidental. Certainly, even non-Shiite Sufism knows of a hidden succession of spiritual Poles. According to Semnânî, for example, the lineage begins before the Prophet of Islam, passes through Mohammad and then the Imams down to the twelfth, and afterward continues through those whom Sufism recognizes in each age as the “Pole of Poles.”

Although this succession represents a displacement of the Shiite idea of the cycle of walâyat, the cycle of spiritual guardianship, it differs from that idea radically: it does not recognize the Twelfth Imam as still present in the world or as permanently holding the position of “Pole of Poles” (Qotb al-aqtâb).

Nor is it the same as the lineage recognized by Sohrawardî, which includes only some of Sufism's “Poles,” because its spiritual ancestry lies elsewhere. We also know that there is general agreement on this point: Ishrâq stands in relation to philosophy as Sufism stands in relation to Kalâm, dialectical, rational, outward-looking theology. The relationship is analogous; Ishrâq and Sufism are not identical.

Nevertheless, the title “Upholder of the Book,” which Sohrawardî gives to his successors, is literally the title borne by the Shiite Imam in relation to the Quran, with the difference that here it refers to the Book of Eastern Theosophy.

Let us turn back, then, to the diagram in which the Shaykh al-Ishrâq sketched the ancestry of the Ishrâqîyûn (above, Chapter I, section 2). There is indeed the idea of a succession, but no document recording it in the archives of a “regularly constituted” association. The matter is “too grave” to be reduced to that. Sohrawardî's project was probably intended to reach far into the future. This is already suggested by the idea of a community of Ishrâq possessing its own “inspired Book,” gathered around its Qâ’im, the one who “possesses the knowledge of the Book.” The model is the Shiite conception.

Yet so far as we know, only Shamsoddîn Shahrazôrî, at the end of his commentary, claimed for himself the title “Upholder of the knowledge of the Book.” What happened after him? Must we suppose that the succession of “Upholders of the Book of Ishrâq” also entered the ghaybat, the state of concealment? In any case, we can still trace a succession of at least some great figures who illustrate the later fortunes of the Book of Eastern Theosophy and its considerable influence in Iran.
2. The Later “Eastern” Tradition in Iran and India
Given the present state of our knowledge and our examination of the texts, we must limit ourselves to a number of landmarks. They are important ones, certainly.

But the influence of the ishrâqî idea upon Iranian thought as a whole cannot be assessed in detail until many texts still surviving only in manuscript have become accessible. The Anthology now in preparation will contribute to that knowledge.

The first name to be placed in the line descending from Sohrawardî's Ishrâq, the line of the “Platonists of Persia,” is that of Shamsoddîn Shahrazôrî. Strangely enough, we know almost nothing about the life of this philosopher, who himself devoted an entire book to the lives of philosophers, both those who lived before Islam and those who appeared within Islam. He is so completely identified with his work that the work alone offers us a few details about the man.

Foremost among his writings are two extensive commentaries on works by Sohrawardî: the Book of Elucidations Inspired by the Tablet and the Throne (Talwîhât) and the Book of Eastern Theosophy. We do know from another source that a young disciple named Shams shared the Shaykh al-Ishrâq's imprisonment in Aleppo. We would like this to have been Shamsoddîn Shahrazôrî himself, Sohrawardî's enthusiastic biographer and commentator.

Yet we cannot even say with certainty that Shahrazôrî had personal contact with Sohrawardî. If he had, why would he have been so hesitant in writing the Shaykh's biography, especially concerning the date of his death? Moreover, he would have had to live an exceptionally long life.

Among his other writings is a monumental encyclopedia entitled Treatises of the Divine Tree and the Theosophical Secrets. It is a Summa of all the philosophy produced within Islam down to his own time, and we can only hope that an editor will soon undertake its publication. The work was completed in 680/1282. Admittedly, this monument, the labor of a lifetime, may have been finished near the end of the author's life.

But a note by a copyist working from the author's original suggests that Shahrazôrî was still alive in 687/1288, a century after Sohrawardî's death. It seems more likely, then, that Shahrazôrî was in contact with Sohrawardî's immediate disciples. His allegiance to Sohrawardî's Ishrâq was all the deeper for having followed a kind of spiritual conversion after an earlier period of reserve.
Another of his books, Hill al-romûz (Solution of the Enigmas), seems to show no trace of Ishrâq at all.

Elsewhere we have described the style and structure of the two great commentaries on Sohrawardî's works and explained why, despite the silence maintained by later commentators on the matter, Shahrazôrî seems to us to come first chronologically. The prologue to his commentary on the Book of Eastern Theosophy bears no dedication. It praises no prince or distinguished person who might have commissioned the work.

There is no hint, then, of a desire to please a patron. The commentary seems entirely inspired by the devotion of mind and heart, given without reservation to an ideal figure. Its only praise is a eulogy of Sohrawardî, following a lament for the decline of the higher sciences and the fading traces of the path followed by the ancient sages, those who had truly experienced theurgic wisdom.

When the Shaykh al-Ishrâq appeared, Shahrazôrî declares, “he undertook to renew what the cycles and ages of time had corrupted, to bring back into view what they had erased ... to raise to life what was dead and abolished.” Philosophy had been completely overwhelmed by Peripatetic thought. The purpose of this book was different. It spoke to the “Solitary Ones” and the “Unique Ones,” individuals set apart from the multitude; that is why it was neglected at first.

“Yet now this eminent man's hour of full noon has come.” Journeys and changes of place have made it possible for men capable of understanding the work to meet one another. Having cleared their hearts of commonplace philosophy, they find themselves increasingly drawn to this singular book. Interest in it grows, “for neither we ourselves nor anyone else have ever encountered a more complete book on theosophical knowledge and the knowledge that initiates into the mysteries.” Such, then, was the wholly disinterested motive that led Shahrazôrî to write his commentary.

One final detail is both significant and revealing. In the preceding pages we have noted Sohrawardî's rather mysterious references to the person who would be the “Upholder of the Book,” or the “Upholder of the knowledge of the Book”—that is, the Book of Eastern Theosophy. This “Upholder” would represent Sohrawardî among those who, in the future, might form something like an Order of the Ishrâqîyûn.

We have also noted that Shiite terminology gives this same title to the Imam as the “Upholder of the Holy Book.” Now Shahrazôrî, unlike the other commentators, does not hesitate to claim the title envisaged by Sohrawardî. His commentary ends with this solemn declaration: “The Upholder of the knowledge of the Book in the present age declares: here ends what, through divine help and inspiration, we have been able to accomplish in commenting upon this sublime book.”

The responsibility and standing Shahrazôrî thus claimed seem to imply an investiture whose origin and meaning remain shrouded in mystery for us. The life of Qotboddîn Shîrâzî, another great commentator on the Book of Eastern Theosophy, can be traced with much greater precision through the written record. He came from Fârs and was born at Shîrâz in 634/1237. His father, Ziyâoddîn Mas’ûd ibn Maslak, originally from Kazerûn, was both a physician and a Sufi Shaykh.

From earliest childhood, then, the future “eminent scholar” (’Allâmeh) was acquainted with scientific learning and the spiritual life. Throughout his life he traveled widely, always seeking scientific and spiritual knowledge; he is recorded as having visited Khorassan, Anatolia, Syria, and Iraq. Among his celebrated teachers were Nasîroddîn Tûsî, the renowned Shiite astronomer and philosopher, and the great mystic Sadroddîn Qonyawî, a disciple and stepson of Ibn ’Arabî. His writings, taken together, have an encyclopedic scope.

Just as Shahrazôrî composed the still-unpublished philosophical encyclopedia mentioned above, so Qotboddîn Shîrâzî produced an encyclopedia embracing the whole system of the sciences. One story reported by Mîrkhond would cast a shadow over our picture of him. He is said to have developed a quiet but stubborn hostility toward his teacher Nasîr Tûsî, to the point of joining a plot to destroy the distinguished philosopher and astronomer's standing with the Mongol ruler Hûlâgû.

The plot failed, since the observatory in which the ruler was so interested had not yet been completed. It is better, with the good Khwânsârî, to doubt that this story concerns the same Qotboddîn, although Khwânsârî adds: “It is true that this would not have been the first bottle to break in Islam.” Our Qotboddîn died at Tabrîz in Ramadan 710/January 1311, at the age of seventy-six lunar years.

His great commentary on the Book of Eastern Theosophy opens with praise of the Shaykh al-Ishrâq no less warm than Shahrazôrî's. He too recalls the mystical theosophy (hikmat dhawqîya, wisdom known through direct experience) of the ancient sages. This included knowledge of the imaginal world through which the resurrection of bodies takes place. It was a knowledge of the divine mysteries and the eternally subsisting Lights, not to be reached through “philosophical chatter” but through a refining and elevation of the innermost consciousness (taltîf al-sirr). Qotboddîn declares that Avicenna had already recalled this in certain passages of his Ishârât.

Then, after lamenting the Peripatetics' excessive resort to dialectical argument—in words reminiscent of both Sohrawardî and Shahrazôrî—Qotboddîn evokes a theosophical wisdom directed toward inward vision, contemplative seeing (moshâhada). This cannot be attained through definitions or syllogisms, but through the Lights that rise in the Orient of the soul (anwâr ishrâqîya), impressing their image upon it as upon a mirror, taking possession of it as fire takes possession of iron heated until it glows. Such was the state of souls “that have sought the Orient and the illumination of the divine Light.” Yet the Shaykh al-Ishrâq's book has remained a hidden treasure. Qotboddîn intends to make the path easier for the soul that longs to put its teachings into practice.

This purpose led him to write a masterly commentary, completed in 694/1295, when he was sixty years old. We recalled earlier that the great encyclopedia into which Shahrazôrî had incorporated the substance of his own commentaries on Sohrawardî was completed in 680/1282. This seems decisive in establishing the chronological priority of Shahrazôrî's commentary. Furthermore, Qotboddîn's commentary includes long passages that reproduce Shahrazôrî's text word for word. It is true, however, that it also contains many developments absent from Shahrazôrî, and its structure is quite different.

Shahrazôrî proceeds by taking relatively long passages of the text as points of departure, inserting his own explanations between them. Qotboddîn, aware of how difficult Sohrawardî's highly compressed text can be, inserts his explanations within the author's very sentences, opening up passages that are too tightly packed before proceeding to the commentary proper. He enriches this with reminders, quotations, and comparisons, making implicit meanings explicit and gradually clearing away every obscurity.

In short, he becomes the best of guides. That is why his annotated edition of the Book of Eastern Theosophy became the standard textbook for every generation of Ishrâqîyûn. Far more manuscripts of it survive than of Shahrazôrî's commentary, which it seems to have pushed into the background—rather as Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî's writings later eclipsed those of his teacher Mîr Dâmâd.

Among the major commentators on Sohrawardî's work, Ibn Kammûna (d. 683/1284) deserves special mention. He wrote an extensive commentary on a work already discussed here, one whose brevity makes it especially difficult: the Book of Elucidations Inspired by the Tablet and the Throne. The work comprises three books, on logic, physics, and metaphysics. It forms the first part of the trilogy that Sohrawardî intended as an indispensable preparation for studying his great Book of Eastern Theosophy. Ibn Kammûna makes no secret of the difficulties he encountered. Had he not been afraid of disappointing those who had asked him to write the commentary, he would have abandoned the undertaking. He completed it in 667/1268.

Yet this commentary, in turn, contains many pages agreeing word for word with Shahrazôrî's commentary on the same treatise by the Shaykh al-Ishrâq. The question arises once again: which writer came first? Elsewhere, in a more detailed account of the work, we have explained why we believe the answer here too must favor Shahrazôrî. This in no way diminishes the importance of Ibn Kammûna's work. His commentary, whose quotations show a thorough knowledge of Sohrawardî's other writings, remains the indispensable aid to close study of the Book of Elucidations that its author intended it to be.

When preparing our edition of Sohrawardî's text more than twenty years ago, we ourselves had access to the copy of Ibn Kammûna's commentary that had belonged to Qotboddîn Shîrâzî, the commentator on the Book of Eastern Theosophy.

We must now be content to name a succession of figures who serve as landmarks. The philosopher Athîroddîn Abharî (d. 663/1265) agreed with thinkers such as Shahrazôrî that the word “metaphysics” (mâ ba’d al-tabî’a, “what comes after physics”) is appropriate only from our human point of view, because we perceive sensible things first.

Thus the priority given to “physics,” the study of natural things or Naturalia, is a matter of convention, not of the nature of things; it reflects a teaching need. In reality, the principles of natural things come before those same natural things in being and in causation. These principles should therefore be established first, within a discipline better called prephysics than metaphysics. Abharî develops this argument in an entire treatise, the Kashf al-haqâ’iq, in which his account of prephysics faithfully reproduces Sohrawardî's ishrâqî philosophy of the human being's existence after death.

As for the writings of the great Shiite philosopher Nasîroddîn Tûsî, mentioned above, it would be interesting to investigate the extent of their debt to Ishrâq. In discussing angelology and the emanation of the Intelligences—which calls into question the famous principle ex uno non fit nisi unum, “from one thing only one thing can proceed”—Mollâ Sadrâ pointed out with great precision what Nasîr Tûsî, in his commentary on Avicenna's Ishârât, owed to Sohrawardî's inward, esoteric application of the laws of optics.

Among Ibn ’Arabî's commentators and disciples, ’Abdorrazzâq Kâshânî (d. around 730/1330) paid particular attention to the Hermetic origins of the Ishrâqîyûn. The influence of Ishrâq is especially striking in the great work of Ibn Abî Jombûr, the Kitâb al-Mojlî, composed in 895/1490, barely ten years before Shâh Isma’îl's accession. Together with the great synthesis of Haydar Âmolî (eighth/fourteenth century), this work brought Shiite theosophy and Ibn ’Arabî's theosophy decisively together. Indeed, it is throughout Ibn ’Arabî's writings that we ought to seek connections with Sohrawardî's Ishrâq.

Later (in Book IV) we shall have occasion to show how Sâ’inoddîn Torkeh Ispahânî, an eminent Shiite philosopher of the fifteenth century (d. 830/1426 or 836/1432) and himself a commentator on Ibn ’Arabî's Fosûs, situated the Ishrâqîyûn. His entire body of work, of great importance for the metaphysics of being, remains to be studied.
